title: Quotient decomposition of a split scalar-extended finite free algebra
statement:
Let $A,C,B$ be commutative rings with homomorphisms $A\to C$ and $A\to B$. Fix an $A$-basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ of $C$, where $d\ge0$ [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. Set $T=C\otimes_A B$, with its $B$-algebra structure through the second factor [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. Let $D$ be a commutative $B$-algebra and let $\theta:T\xrightarrow{\sim}B\times D$ be a $B$-algebra isomorphism. Assume that an $A$-algebra homomorphism $f:C\to B$ satisfies $\operatorname{pr}_1\theta(c\otimes b)=f(c)b$ for every $c\in C,b\in B$. For an ideal $K\subset C$, let $KB\subset B$ be generated by $f(K)$, let $J\subset T$ be generated as an ideal by $k\otimes1$ for $k\in K$, and let $H\subset D$ be generated as an ideal by $\operatorname{pr}_2\theta(k\otimes1)$ for $k\in K$. Then $v_i=e_i\otimes1$ form a $B$-basis of $T$, and
$$J=\operatorname{span}_B\{k\otimes1:k\in K\},\qquad \theta(J)=KB\times H.$$
The canonical quotient map identifies $(C/K)\otimes_A B$ with $T/J$. There is a $B$-linear isomorphism
$$(C/K)\otimes_A B\xrightarrow{\sim}(B/KB)\oplus(D/H)$$
sending $(c\bmod K)\otimes b$ to $(f(c)b\bmod KB,\operatorname{pr}_2\theta(c\otimes b)\bmod H)$. The $B$-modules $D$, $D/H$, $B/KB$ and $(C/K)\otimes_A B$ are finitely generated [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. No finite generation of $K$ and no flatness of $B$ over $A$ are assumed.

source.place: Tag 0812 (lemma-trick-fitting-ideal), proof, passage from the algebra product decomposition to the quotient module decomposition; finite free base change and the product ideal identification made explicit.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-free-module-base-change-free] with $R=A$, scalar algebra $B$ and free module $C$. Its right-factor version gives the $B$-basis $v_i=e_i\otimes1$ of $T$, including when the index set is empty.

source.place: Tag 0812 (lemma-trick-fitting-ideal), proof: the algebra product decomposition and the following quotient module decomposition, with the implicit elementary algebra written out.

proof.text: Put $S=\operatorname{span}_B\{k\otimes1:k\in K\}$. Pure tensors generate $T$ by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The multiplication formula of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property] gives $(c\otimes b)(k\otimes1)=b\cdot(ck\otimes1)\in S$ since $ck\in K$. Distributing over finite sums shows that $S$ is an ideal of $T$. Thus $J\subset S$ by the definition of the generated ideal, while $S\subset J$ since an ideal of the $B$-algebra $T$ is closed under $B$-scalar multiplication. Hence $J=S$.

source.place: Tag 0812 (lemma-trick-fitting-ideal), proof: the algebra product decomposition and the following quotient module decomposition, with the implicit elementary algebra written out.

proof.text: Write $g(k)=\operatorname{pr}_2\theta(k\otimes1)$. Since $\theta$ is a surjective ring isomorphism, $\theta(J)$ is the ideal of $B\times D$ generated by $(f(k),g(k))$, $k\in K$: images and inverse images of the finite sums defining a generated ideal give both inclusions. Every such sum lies in $KB\times H$. Conversely multiply each generator by $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ to get $(f(k),0)$ and $(0,g(k))$. Multiplying these by $(b,0)$ and $(0,d)$, then adding, gives every pair in $KB\times H$ by the definitions of $KB$ and $H$. Therefore $\theta(J)=KB\times H$.

source.place: Tag 0812 (lemma-trick-fitting-ideal), proof: the algebra product decomposition and the following quotient module decomposition, with the implicit elementary algebra written out.

proof.text: Construct the quotient comparison explicitly. The maps $C\to(C/K)\otimes_A B$, $c\mapsto\bar c\otimes1$, and $B\to(C/K)\otimes_A B$, $b\mapsto1\otimes b$, induce $\beta:T\to(C/K)\otimes_A B$ by [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. It kills every $k\otimes1$, hence $J$, so $\bar\beta:T/J\to(C/K)\otimes_A B$, $[t]\mapsto\beta(t)$, is well-defined. In the other direction $C/K\to T/J$, $\bar c\mapsto[c\otimes1]$, is well-defined since changing $c$ by $k\in K$ changes its value by $[k\otimes1]=0$; it is an $A$-algebra map, as is $B\to T/J$, $b\mapsto[1\otimes b]$. The same universal property gives $\alpha:(C/K)\otimes_A B\to T/J$ with $\alpha(\bar c\otimes b)=[c\otimes b]$. The quotient algebra structures are those of [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. The composites fix all pure tensors, which generate by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], and their images in $T/J$. Thus $\alpha$ and $\bar\beta$ are inverse $B$-algebra maps; $B$-linearity also follows directly on pure tensors from multiplication in their second factors.

source.place: Tag 0812 (lemma-trick-fitting-ideal), proof: the algebra product decomposition and the following quotient module decomposition, with the implicit elementary algebra written out.

proof.text: Define $\gamma:T/J\to(B/KB)\oplus(D/H)$ by $[t]\mapsto([\operatorname{pr}_1\theta(t)],[\operatorname{pr}_2\theta(t)])$, using the quotient structures of [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. Step 3 makes this well-defined. Its inverse is $([b],[d])\mapsto[\theta^{-1}(b,d)]$: changing representatives by $(x,y)\in KB\times H=\theta(J)$ changes the result by an element of $J$. The two formulas are inverse and $B$-linear because $\theta$ is a $B$-algebra isomorphism. Here the two-term direct sum is the module of pairs. Composing $\gamma$ with $\alpha$ gives the claimed isomorphism and, on $\bar c\otimes b$, exactly $([f(c)b],[\operatorname{pr}_2\theta(c\otimes b)])$.

source.place: Tag 0812 (lemma-trick-fitting-ideal), proof: the algebra product decomposition and the following quotient module decomposition, with the implicit elementary algebra written out.

proof.text: The $d$ elements $\operatorname{pr}_2\theta(v_i)$ generate $D$: lift $d_0\in D$ to $\theta^{-1}(0,d_0)$, expand it in the basis $(v_i)$, and project the expansion. Their residue classes generate $D/H$. The single class of $1$ generates $B/KB$. The $d$ elements $\alpha^{-1}([v_i])$ generate $(C/K)\otimes_A B$, since any representative in $T$ has a basis expansion and $\alpha^{-1}$ is $B$-linear. These are finite generating lists in the sense of [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Every calculation used finite sums representing individual elements, so no finite generating list for $K$ and no flatness of $B$ over $A$ was used.
